samples.text: Floating-point addition is not associative because the order in which numbers are added can affect the result due to rounding errors that occur when numbers of different magnitudes are added together. For example, adding a very large number to a very small number can result in the small number being rounded to zero, leading to different results depending on the order of operations. This non-associativity can lead to unexpected behavior in certain calculations, such as when summing a series of numbers with varying magnitudes, where the final result depends on the order in which the numbers are added.

Floating-point addition is not associative because the order in which numbers are added can affect the result due to rounding errors that occur when numbers of significantly different magnitudes are added together. For example, adding a very small number to a very large number may result in the small number being rounded away, but the order in which these numbers are added can change whether this rounding occurs before or after other additions, leading to different final results. As a result, the expression `(a + b) + c` can produce a different result than `a + (b + c)`, even when `a`, `b`, and `c` are all finite floating-point numbers, demonstrating the non-associativity of floating-point addition.
